title: General truths
theme: Zero conditional (general truths, facts, instructions) + contrast with first conditional
goal: Student uses zero conditional for universal truths, scientific facts, and rules; distinguishes from first conditional (specific future) and knows when to use "when" vs "if".
connects_to: M11 (Time clauses) — after zero/first conditional, expand to before/after/until/by the time.
module_chunks: If + present, will + base (first — specific future)
If you heat water, it boils.
When the sun sets, it gets dark.
If you don't water plants, they die.

units.title: General truths
units.grammar_focus: Zero conditional (If + present, present) for facts
units.real_life_context: You express scientific facts, life rules, and cause-effect that's always true.

grammar.sentence: If you heat water to 100 degrees, it _____.
grammar.explanation: Zero conditional describes truths that are always valid. Both clauses use present simple. "Boils" — universal fact about water.

grammar.sentence: If you mix red and blue, you _____ purple.
grammar.explanation: Color is a universal result. Zero conditional = cause-effect that always happens. Present simple in both clauses.

grammar.sentence: If it _____, plants grow faster.
grammar.explanation: "If it rains" — present simple third person (it + verb-s). Universal truth about plant growth.

grammar.sentence: Ice _____ if you heat it.
grammar.explanation: A zero conditional can start with either clause. "Ice melts if you heat it" — physical fact.

grammar.sentence: If you don't sleep enough, you _____ tired the next day.
grammar.explanation: Always-true consequence. Common verbs: feel, get, become — all in present simple.

grammar.sentence: When the temperature _____ zero degrees, water freezes.
grammar.explanation: "When" works like "if" in general truths — both signal an always-true relationship. "Drops to zero" — 3rd person singular.

grammar.sentence: If you don't water plants, they _____.
grammar.explanation: "They die" — plural plants use the base form of the verb. Universal consequence of not watering.

grammar.sentence: If you heat water, it will boil.
grammar.hint: Zero conditional para verdades gerais não usa "will"
grammar.answer: If you heat water, it boils.
grammar.explanation: "Will" shifts the meaning to a specific prediction (first conditional). For always-true facts, both clauses stay in present simple.

grammar.sentence: If you mixing red and blue, you get purple.
grammar.answer: If you mix red and blue, you get purple.
grammar.explanation: The "if" clause needs a complete present simple: "mix" (base form with you), not "mixing". The -ing form would require "are mixing" (present continuous).

grammar.passage: If you heat water, it boils. When the sun sets, it gets dark. If you don't drink water, you get dehydrated. Plants die if you don't water them.
grammar.question: What happens when the sun sets?
grammar.explanation: The text says "When the sun sets, it gets dark" — universal truth about day/night cycle.

listening_speaking.text: If you heat water, it boils.
If you mix red and blue, you get purple.
Ice melts if you heat it.
When the sun sets, it gets dark.
If you don't sleep, you feel tired.

units.title: Zero vs first
units.grammar_focus: Distinguishing zero conditional (general truth) from first conditional (specific future)
units.real_life_context: You choose the right conditional based on whether you're talking about always-true facts or specific future possibilities.

grammar.sentence: "If you study every day, you _____ better." (general truth)
grammar.explanation: "Every day" signals an always-true pattern → zero conditional. Studying regularly always improves performance. Present simple in both clauses.

grammar.sentence: "If you study tonight, you _____ better on tomorrow's test." (specific future)
grammar.explanation: "Tonight" + "tomorrow's test" signal a specific future event → first conditional. Use "will + base" in the consequence.

grammar.sentence: If you don't water plants, they _____ — that's how nature works.
grammar.explanation: "That's how nature works" signals a universal truth → zero conditional. "Plants die" — present simple plural.

grammar.sentence: If it _____ tomorrow, I'll stay home.
grammar.explanation: After "if", always present simple — even in first conditional. "Tomorrow" elsewhere in the sentence marks a specific event. "It rains" — 3rd person.

grammar.sentence: Water _____ when you heat it to 100 degrees.
grammar.explanation: Universal truth about water. "Boils" — 3rd person singular present simple. "When" works like "if" in general truths.

grammar.sentence: I _____ go to the beach if it's sunny on Saturday.
grammar.explanation: "On Saturday" = specific event → first conditional. "I'll go" or "I will go" in the future consequence.

grammar.sentence: If you exercise regularly, you _____ healthier — it's a fact.
grammar.explanation: "It's a fact" reinforces a general truth → zero conditional. The consequence also stays in present simple.

grammar.sentence: If I will have time tomorrow, I'll call you.
grammar.hint: Após "if", nunca usar "will" — sempre present simple
grammar.answer: If I have time tomorrow, I'll call you.
grammar.explanation: The "if" clause is ALWAYS in present simple, even in first conditional. "Will" only appears in the consequence. This is one of the most common errors for Portuguese speakers.

grammar.sentence: "If you heat water, it will boil." (para descrever verdade geral)
grammar.answer: If you heat water, it boils.
grammar.explanation: "Will boil" suggests a specific prediction. For an always-true fact, use present simple in both clauses: "it boils".

grammar.passage: If you don't water plants, they die — that's how nature works. If it rains tomorrow, I'll stay home and read. Plants need sunlight to grow, and if they don't get it, they wither.
grammar.question: What will the speaker do if it rains tomorrow?
grammar.explanation: The text says "If it rains tomorrow, I'll stay home and read" — first conditional with specific future plan.

listening_speaking.text: If you study every day, you get better.

If you don't water plants, they die.
If it rains tomorrow, I'll stay home.
Water boils when you heat it to 100.

units.title: When vs If
units.grammar_focus: When (certainty/routine) vs If (possibility) in conditional contexts
units.real_life_context: You choose between "when" and "if" based on how certain or uncertain the situation is.

grammar.sentence: "_____ the sun rises, it gets light." (it always happens)
grammar.explanation: The sun always rises — it isn't uncertain. "When" is used for certain events that always happen.

grammar.sentence: "_____ it rains tomorrow, I'll take an umbrella." (uncertain)
grammar.explanation: Tomorrow's rain is UNCERTAIN — it may or may not happen. "If" for possible but not guaranteed events.

grammar.sentence: _____ I wake up, the first thing I do is check my phone.
grammar.explanation: Waking up is part of the routine — it always happens. "When I wake up" signals temporal certainty.

grammar.sentence: _____ you're feeling tired, you should rest.
grammar.explanation: Both work — "If" emphasizes possibility, "When" emphasizes that whenever it happens, do X. In advice, both are natural.

grammar.sentence: _____ winter comes, the days get shorter.
grammar.explanation: Winter is a guaranteed yearly event — use "when". "If winter comes" would sound odd because winter always arrives.

grammar.sentence: _____ you don't feel well, take a break.
grammar.explanation: You aren't always sick — it varies. "If you don't feel well" — possibility.

grammar.sentence: _____ I get home from work, I take off my shoes and sit down.
grammar.explanation: Getting home from work is part of the routine. "When I get home" — every time it happens.

grammar.sentence: If the sun rises, the day starts.
grammar.answer: When the sun rises, the day starts.
grammar.explanation: Guaranteed natural events use "when". "If" suggests doubt — will the sun rise? Of course it will.

grammar.sentence: "When it snows tomorrow, I'll build a snowman." (incerto)
grammar.answer: If it snows tomorrow, I'll build a snowman.
grammar.explanation: Uncertain future events call for "if". "When" would only work if you were absolutely sure it'll snow.

grammar.passage: When the sun rises, the day begins. If it rains tomorrow, I'll stay inside. When I wake up, I have coffee. If you ever visit my city, I'll show you around.
grammar.question: What does the speaker do when they wake up?
grammar.explanation: The text says "When I wake up, I have coffee" — routine that always happens.

listening_speaking.text: When the sun rises, it gets light.
If it rains tomorrow, I'll take an umbrella.
When I wake up, I check my phone.
If you're tired, you should rest.

units.title: Conditional review
units.real_life_context: You mix general truths and specific predictions naturally in the same conversation.

grammar.sentence: "If I _____ time tomorrow, I'll go to the gym." (specific future)
grammar.explanation: First conditional: "if + present simple, will + base". After "if", never "will". "Tomorrow" marks a specific future.

grammar.sentence: "Water _____ if heated to 100." (general truth)
grammar.explanation: Universal truth about water → zero conditional. Present simple in both clauses.

grammar.sentence: "If you _____ hard, you'll succeed in life." (motivational)
grammar.explanation: After "if", present simple "work". The consequence "succeed" takes "will" — motivational first conditional.

grammar.sentence: "When I _____ home, I cook dinner." (routine)
grammar.explanation: Daily routine → "when + present, present". "I get home and cook" — always true.

grammar.sentence: If I _____ early enough, I'll have breakfast at home.
grammar.explanation: "Wake up" — fixed phrasal verb in present simple. First conditional signals a specific future result.

grammar.sentence: Plants die if you don't _____ them regularly.
grammar.explanation: Universal truth about plants → zero conditional. "If you don't water them" — negative present simple with "you".

grammar.sentence: I'll be there if you _____ me to be.
grammar.explanation: First conditional with a promise. "Want" — present simple base form with "you".

grammar.sentence: If it will rain tomorrow, I'll stay home.
grammar.answer: If it rains tomorrow, I'll stay home.
grammar.explanation: Core rule: the "if" clause is ALWAYS in present simple, even in first conditional. "Will" only in the consequence.

grammar.sentence: If you heat water, it will boils.
grammar.hint: Verdade geral usa present simple em ambas cláusulas, sem "will" e sem -s extra
grammar.answer: If you heat water, it boils.
grammar.explanation: For a universal truth, zero conditional. "It boils" — present simple 3rd person. "Will boils" doesn't exist — after "will" comes the base form (boil).

grammar.passage: If you study consistently, you learn faster — that's universal. If I have free time this weekend, I'll catch up on reading. Plants need water; if they don't get it, they die. When it gets dark, I usually feel sleepy.
grammar.question: What does the speaker plan to do this weekend?
grammar.explanation: The text says "If I have free time this weekend, I'll catch up on reading" — specific future plan.

listening_speaking.text: If I have time tomorrow, I'll go to the gym.
Water boils if heated.
If you work hard, you'll succeed.
When I get home, I cook dinner.
If I wake up early, I'll have a big breakfast.

units.title: Conditionals in context
units.grammar_focus: Full integration of zero + first conditionals in natural conversation
units.real_life_context: You speak conditionally without thinking — mixing truths, plans, and possibilities seamlessly.

grammar.sentence: "If you _____ this medicine, you'll feel better." (specific advice)
grammar.explanation: First conditional: "if + present simple, will + base". Após "if" nunca "will".

grammar.sentence: "Water _____ at zero degrees Celsius." (fact)
grammar.explanation: Universal scientific fact → present simple. "Water freezes" — 3rd person.

grammar.sentence: "If you _____ ice, it melts." (general truth)
grammar.explanation: Universal truth → zero conditional. "If you heat" — present simple with "you".

grammar.sentence: "I _____ help you if you ask me to." (offer)
grammar.explanation: First conditional with an offer. "I will help" — conditional promise.

grammar.sentence: If I _____ free time this evening, I'll watch a movie.
grammar.explanation: First conditional. "Have free time" — present simple.

grammar.sentence: Plants _____ if you don't water them — that's biology.
grammar.explanation: Universal biological truth → zero conditional. "Plants die" — plural present simple.

grammar.sentence: _____ you study consistently, you make progress.
grammar.explanation: Both work in universal truths. "If/When you study consistently".

grammar.sentence: "If I have time, I travel a lot." (sentido específico de "este ano")
grammar.answer: If I have time, I'll travel a lot.
grammar.explanation: If the context is a specific future plan, you need "will" in the consequence. Without "will", it sounds like a general truth (whenever I have time, I travel).

grammar.sentence: If you will be late, please call me.
grammar.answer: If you are late, please call me.
grammar.explanation: The "if" clause is ALWAYS present simple — even when the sentence is about the future. "If you are" — present simple.

grammar.passage: If you take this medicine three times a day, you'll feel better in a week. If I finish work early tomorrow, I'll join you for dinner. When water freezes, it expands — that's why pipes burst in winter.
grammar.question: When will the speaker join for dinner?
grammar.answer: if I finish work early tomorrow
grammar.explanation: The text says "If I finish work early tomorrow, I'll join you for dinner" — first conditional with specific plan.

listening_speaking.text: If you take this medicine, you'll feel better.
Water freezes at zero degrees.
If you heat ice, it melts.
I'll help you if you ask me to.
If I have time, I'll travel.
